title: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
summary: How SGLang co-designs a Python frontend and a runtime: radix-tree KV reuse extended to host memory, prefix-aware queue order, grammar masks, an overlapped scheduler, cache-aware routing, PD and speculation.
outcomes: Explain how the frontend primitives (gen, select, fork) expose shared prefixes and parallelism to the runtime
Trace radix tree match, split, insert and LRU leaf eviction, and compute hit rates on a request trace
Trace how HiCache demotes evicted radix nodes to host memory, and compare load and recompute cost
Explain why longest-prefix-first ordering reaches the DFS-optimal hit rate, and when it starves requests
Count the passes jump-forward saves, and explain where SGLang compiles grammars and builds token masks
Explain the overlap scheduler's future-token buffer, chunked prefill and CUDA graph padding, and read server logs
Describe TP, DP, DP attention, EP and sgl-router's KV-event cache-aware routing, and compute DP attention costs
Configure PD disaggregation and EAGLE speculation in SGLang, and predict when each one helps

lessons.title: LM programs: why the runtime should see the whole program

blocks.md: Many LLM applications are not one prompt and one answer. An agent plans, calls a tool, and calls the model again; a judge forks a prompt into several parallel evaluations and merges them; a few-shot benchmark sends thousands of prompts that start with the same examples. The SGLang paper (Zheng et al., published at NeurIPS 2024, the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems) calls these **LM programs**: several generation calls mixed with control flow, with structured inputs and outputs.

The paper names two costs of running LM programs on an engine that sees each request in isolation:

- **Redundant prefill.** Calls in one program share long prefixes (the same system prompt, the same chat history, the same few-shot examples), yet engines of the time threw the KV cache away when a request finished, so every call recomputed it.
- **Slow structured output.** Constrained decoding (for example, JSON that must match a schema) was done one token per forward pass, even where the format leaves only one possible continuation.

SGLang answers with two parts that can be used together or separately: a **frontend language** embedded in Python, and a **runtime** (SRT, the SGLang Runtime) with RadixAttention for KV reuse and a compressed finite state machine for faster constrained decoding. The frontend primitives are:

- `gen` calls the model and stores the result under a name; it accepts `regex` to constrain the output.
- `select` picks the most probable option from a list.
- `+=` (extend) appends text to the prompt state; `s["name"]` reads a result.
- `fork` makes parallel copies of the prompt state; `join` merges them.
- `image` and `video` add multimodal inputs.

blocks.code:
import sglang as sgl

@sgl.function
def tip_suggestion(s):
    s += ("Here are two tips for staying healthy: "
          "1. Balanced Diet. 2. Regular Exercise.\n\n")
    forks = s.fork(2)                      # two copies of the prompt state
    for i, f in enumerate(forks):
        f += f"Now, expand tip {i + 1} into a paragraph:\n"
        f += sgl.gen("detailed_tip", max_tokens=256, stop="\n\n")
    s += "Tip 1:" + forks[0]["detailed_tip"] + "\n"   # blocks until ready
    s += "Tip 2:" + forks[1]["detailed_tip"] + "\n"
    s += "In summary" + sgl.gen("summary")

sgl.set_default_backend(sgl.RuntimeEndpoint("http://localhost:30000"))
state = tip_suggestion.run()
print(state["summary"])
blocks.caption: Adapted from the repo's frontend examples. Each fork shares the first sentence as a prefix; the final summary call shares it too.

blocks.md: The **interpreter** treats each prompt state as an asynchronous stream. A `gen` is submitted to the stream and Python keeps running, much like launching a CUDA kernel; only reading a result such as `forks[0]["detailed_tip"]` blocks. CUDA is NVIDIA's platform for programming GPUs, and launching a kernel (a function that runs on the GPU) only queues the work: the CPU call returns at once and keeps going while the GPU computes. So the loop above submits both branches before either finishes, and the runtime batches them. A program can also be traced into a dataflow graph (compiler mode), which the paper limits to programs without data-dependent control flow.

blocks.title: How tip_suggestion reaches the runtime

scenes.caption: The program starts with one prompt state holding the shared instruction text.
At fork, the interpreter first sends the shared prefix to the runtime as a hint, so it is computed once and inserted into the radix tree before the branches arrive.
Both branches are submitted without waiting. Each one matches the cached prefix and only prefills its own short instruction.
Reading the fork results blocks until both are done. The summary prompt still begins with the original prefix, so its KV is reused a third time.

blocks.prompt: A program calls `gen` three times in sequence on the same state `s`, each time appending to the previous text. On an engine that frees the KV cache when each request ends, how many times is the original prompt prefilled? And with RadixAttention?
blocks.reveal: On the old engine, **three times**: each call is a new request whose prompt starts with the full original text plus everything generated so far, and nothing survives between requests. With RadixAttention the first call's prompt and output stay in the tree, so the second and third calls prefill only the text appended since the previous call. The longer the shared history, the bigger the saving.

blocks.md: The runtime does not need the frontend. It serves OpenAI-compatible and native HTTP APIs, and RadixAttention matches prefixes of whatever prompts arrive, from any client. The frontend adds information the runtime cannot guess, such as fork hints and intra-program parallelism. For API-only models (for example OpenAI's), where the runtime is out of reach, SGLang offers **API speculative execution**: the first `gen` is allowed to run past its stop string, and the interpreter reuses the extra text for later `gen` calls when it matches the template, saving a call's input-token cost.

SGLang's starting point is **co-design**: the program knows its structure (shared prefixes, forks, output formats), and the runtime turns that structure into skipped prefill and fewer decoding steps. In the paper's ablation (an experiment that switches off one component at a time to measure what each one contributes), turning off frontend parallelism or frontend hints lowered performance even with every runtime optimization on.

Misconception: "SGLang is a prompt DSL, so I must rewrite my app to use it." A DSL, or domain-specific language, is a small language built for one kind of job, here writing LM programs. Most of SGLang's speedups live in the runtime and apply to plain HTTP requests. The DSL is an optional layer on top.

blocks.question: In `tip_suggestion`, what happens when Python executes `f += sgl.gen(...)` for fork 0?
options: Python blocks until fork 0's paragraph is fully generated, then moves to fork 1
Both forks are concatenated into a single request with one long prompt
The call is submitted to fork 0's stream and returns at once, so fork 1 is submitted right away and the runtime can batch them
The function is compiled into a CUDA graph before any request is sent
blocks.explain: The interpreter runs each prompt state as an asynchronous stream: `gen` is non-blocking, like a kernel launch. Only reading a result (`forks[0]["detailed_tip"]`) waits. That is what gives intra-program parallelism.

blocks.question: Why does the interpreter send the shared prefix to the runtime before the fork branches?
options: So that the prefix is computed and inserted into the radix tree once; branches arriving together would otherwise each find nothing cached and each prefill it
Because the runtime cannot accept prompts longer than the prefix
To let the runtime pick a different model for each branch
Because RadixAttention only works when requests arrive one at a time
blocks.explain: If both branches arrive at the same moment with nothing cached, each matches zero tokens and each computes the shared part. The paper calls the fix a frontend hint: it simplifies runtime matching and is one of the co-design benefits in its ablation.

lessons.title: RadixAttention: matching, splitting and evicting prefixes

blocks.md: Recall from the prerequisite: a paged KV pool stores each token's keys and values in slots reached through an index, and prefix caching reuses those slots when a new prompt starts with tokens already computed. The prerequisite already sketched SGLang's **RadixAttention**; here it is traced in code. It keeps finished requests' prompts *and outputs* in a radix tree: a trie whose edges hold whole token runs. Each path from the root spells a cached prefix and points at its KV slots. The paper uses a page size of one token, and `--page-size` still defaults to 1. Token-sized pages are practical because the attention kernels gather scattered KV: FlashInfer, for example, treats the page table as a block-sparse matrix whose blocks are one token wide and copies the scattered rows into on-chip memory before the dense math (the *FlashInfer* course, optional reading outside this course's prerequisites, measures what that costs; lesson 7 lists SGLang's attention backends).

A radix cache needs only three operations. **Match** walks from the root, comparing tokens, and returns how many leading tokens are cached. **Insert** adds the uncached rest as a new leaf. When a prompt diverges in the middle of an edge, that edge is **split** in two so both paths can share the common part. The code below is a 39-line model of match and insert, run on character tokens.

blocks.title: Match, split and insert on a tiny radix tree
blocks.code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key = key        # tokens on the edge into this node
        self.children = {}    # first token -> child node
        self.ref = 0          # running requests using this node

def common_len(a, b):
    k = 0
    while k < len(a) and k < len(b) and a[k] == b[k]:
        k += 1
    return k

def split(parent, child, k):
    mid = Node(child.key[:k])
    parent.children[mid.key[0]] = mid
    child.key = child.key[k:]
    mid.children[child.key[0]] = child
    return mid

def match(root, tokens):
    node, n = root, 0
    while n < len(tokens) and tokens[n] in node.children:
        child = node.children[tokens[n]]
        k = common_len(child.key, tokens[n:])
        if k < len(child.key):
            child = split(node, child, k)
        node, n = child, n + k
    return n, node

def insert(root, tokens):
    n, node = match(root, tokens)
    if n < len(tokens):
        node.children[tokens[n]] = Node(tokens[n:])
    return n

root = Node("")
print(insert(root, "ABCD"))
print(insert(root, "ABXY"))
print(match(root, "ABCE")[0])

scenes.caption: Insert ABCD into an empty tree. The root has no children, so match returns 0 and the whole sequence becomes one leaf edge.
Insert ABXY. Match follows the child that starts with A and compares the edge ABCD with ABXY: they agree on 2 tokens.
Only 2 of the edge's 4 tokens matched, so the edge is split into AB and CD. AB is now an inner node that both prompts can share.
Match stops at AB (no child starts with X) and returns 2. Insert hangs the uncached tail XY under AB. Two cached prompts now share the KV of A and B.
A lookup for ABCE matches AB fully, then 1 token of CD, so CD splits into C and D. The answer is 3: only E would need prefill.

blocks.md:
Two rules keep the cache safe while requests run:

- **Reference counts.** Every node counts the running requests that use it. A request locks the whole path from its matched node to the root, and only nodes with count 0 can be evicted.
- **Leaves first, least recently used first.** Eviction removes the LRU unlocked leaf; its parent may then become a leaf and compete in turn. Evicting an inner node first would strand its descendants, whose KV is useless without the prefix.

There is no reserved cache region: cached tokens and running requests share one pool, so under heavy load the cache shrinks to make room for a bigger batch. The tree itself lives on the CPU; the paper measured 0.2 s of tree upkeep in a 74.3 s run with no reuse at all.

blocks.caption: The paper's definition. Output tokens are not counted, though they are inserted and can be reused by a later turn.

blocks.md: Now a trace. Two chat sessions share a 300-token system prompt; user turns are 40 to 60 tokens and replies 80 to 100. A few-shot batch shares 500 tokens of examples plus a 30-token question and a 5-token answer. The eight requests run one at a time (simplified: no batching), and each finished prompt and output is inserted. A script ran the tree above, with LRU leaf eviction, at three cache capacities.

blocks.title: Prefill tokens computed per request (radix tree simulation)

scenes.caption: No reuse: every request prefills its whole prompt, 3910 tokens in total. Later chat turns grow because they resend the history.
Unlimited cache: B reuses the system prompt, each chat turn reuses its own history, and q2 and q3 reuse the 500 example tokens. Only 1130 tokens are computed: a 71.1% hit rate.

Capacity 1200 tokens. Few-shot q1 needs room, and the LRU leaf is B's first turn, so B turn 2 reuses only the system prompt (190 computed). Running B turn 2 then evicts A's history: A turn 3 computes 330. Hit rate 60.1%.
Capacity 900 tokens. Once both chat histories are gone, the 300-token system prompt is itself an LRU leaf, and q3 evicts it to free 5 tokens. B turn 2 now hits nothing. Hit rate 52.4%.

blocks.prompt: Before the last scene: going from 1200 to 900 tokens of cache, how many cached tokens do you expect B turn 2 to reuse? It reused 300 at 1200.
blocks.reveal: **Zero.** At 900 tokens, few-shot q1 forces out both chat histories, which leaves the system prompt node with no children: it is now a leaf. Its last use (A turn 2) is older than the few-shot nodes, so when q3 needs 5 more tokens, LRU evicts the whole 300-token node. Eviction removes a node at a time, so a small request can evict a large prefix.

blocks.md: A shared prefix is not pinned. It is protected only while running requests hold it or while cached descendants keep it an inner node. Once it becomes a leaf it competes on recency like any other leaf. The current docs offer other scorings (`lfu`, least frequently used, which evicts the leaf with the fewest hits; `slru`, segmented least recently used, which moves entries hit twice into a protected segment evicted last; and `priority`) through `--radix-eviction-policy`; `lru` is the default.

With `--page-size` above 1, matches are rounded down to whole pages: a 100-token shared prefix with 16-token pages reuses 96 tokens. Larger pages suit some attention kernels; a page size of 1 reuses every matching token.

blocks.question: In the 1200-token run, B turn 1 finished and was inserted, yet B turn 2 reused only 300 tokens. Why?
options: B turn 2 used a different system prompt
When few-shot q1 needed room, B's turn-1 leaf was the least recently used unlocked leaf, so it was evicted
Radix trees cannot store model outputs
B turn 2 was longer than the cache capacity
blocks.explain: LRU looks at last use. A turn 2 had touched A's branch more recently, and the few-shot nodes did not exist yet, so B's leaf (user turn plus reply, 140 tokens) went first. The system prompt survived because A's branch still hung below it.

blocks.question: Which statement about evicting an inner node before its children is right?
options: It is fine, because children store their own copy of the prefix KV
It frees more memory and is preferred under pressure
It would leave the children unreachable: their KV is only usable together with the prefix, so the memory would be wasted
It is required whenever a node's reference count is above 0
blocks.explain: A cached suffix's keys and values were computed attending to its prefix, and lookups always walk from the root. Without the prefix the suffix can never be matched, so leaves-first is the only eviction order that never strands KV.

lessons.title: HiCache: a radix tree that spans GPU, host memory and storage

blocks.md:
In the 900-token run of the last lesson, few-shot q3 evicted the 300-token system prompt to free 5 tokens, and B turn 2 then recomputed all 490 of its prompt tokens. Those bytes did not have to vanish. A GPU server's **host memory** (the ordinary CPU DRAM next to it) is usually several times larger than the GPU memory left for KV.

**HiCache**, SGLang's hierarchical cache, keeps the radix tree but lets each node's KV live in up to three tiers, named after CPU caches: **L1** GPU memory, **L2** host memory, **L3** a storage backend. Eviction from the GPU can then **demote** a node to host memory instead of deleting it, and a later match loads it back.

Each node of the **HiRadixTree** still holds a run of tokens, and now also records where its KV lives: L1, L2, L3, or several at once. For L1 and L2 it keeps exact addresses. For L3 it keeps nothing: it asks the backend at request time, because keeping metadata in sync with a shared store would cost too much. Three operations follow:

- **Local match** walks the tree and returns one contiguous prefix whose first part is on the GPU and the rest in host memory.
- **Prefetch** asks L3 for the pages after that prefix and copies them into host memory, if at least 256 tokens hit (the default threshold).
- **Write-back** copies new KV down a tier after prefill.

When is KV copied down? `--hicache-write-policy` picks one of three:

- `write_through` (the default at the pinned commit): a node is copied to the next tier as soon as it is cached.
- `write_through_selective`: copied only once it has been hit again (the code uses a threshold of 2 accesses instead of 1), so one-off prefixes cost no copy.
- `write_back`: copied only when evicted from the tier above, so the GPU slot is reused only after the copy finishes.

The *KV cache offloading* course, optional reading outside this course's prerequisites, compares these with other systems' admission rules. Here we rerun lesson 2's trace with write_through.

blocks.title: The 900-token trace again, with a 2,000-token host tier

scenes.caption: After A's second turn: four nodes, 730 tokens, all on the GPU. Under write_through each was also copied to host memory as soon as it was cached (G+H).
Few-shot q1 needs 535 slots. The LRU GPU leaves B1, A1 and A2 lose their GPU copies but stay in the tree as host-only nodes. The plain cache deleted them.
q3 needs 35 more slots and the system prompt is now the LRU GPU leaf. It is demoted too: the 300 tokens the plain cache threw away wait in host memory.
B turn 2 matches sys plus B1, 440 tokens, all in host memory. They are loaded back to the GPU and only 50 tokens are prefilled, not 490. The few-shot nodes are demoted to make room.
A turn 3: sys is on the GPU, A1 and A2 (290 tokens) come back from host memory, 40 tokens are prefilled. B2 is demoted. Host memory now holds 1,605 tokens.

blocks.title: Prefill tokens per request at 900 GPU tokens (simulation)

scenes.caption: Plain radix cache at 900 tokens (lesson 2): 1,860 tokens computed, a 52.4% hit rate. B turn 2 and A turn 3 pay for evicted history.
Same GPU capacity plus a 2,000-token host tier: 1,130 tokens computed, a 71.1% hit rate, exactly what an unlimited cache achieved in lesson 2.
The price: tokens copied from host memory back to the GPU, 440 for B turn 2 and 290 for A turn 3. With a 1,200-token host tier only 300 come back and the hit rate is 60.1%.

blocks.md:
Is loading really cheaper than recomputing? Take the cost model of the *KV cache offloading* course (optional reading, not a prerequisite; everything needed is restated here): Llama 3 8B with 128 KiB of KV per token, prefill at an assumed 400 TFLOPS and a host link at an assumed 50 GB/s. Loading costs 131,072 bytes over 50 GB/s, 2.6 microseconds per token. Recomputing costs at least $2P/F$, 34.9 microseconds per token, where $P$ = 6.98e9 is the number of weights in the linear layers, and more as attention grows.

For the trace (a script computed both): B turn 2's 440 host tokens take 15.5 ms to recompute and 1.15 ms to load; A turn 3's 290 tokens at positions 300 to 589 take 10.3 ms versus 0.76 ms. Both are about 13x cheaper to load. HiCache also hides much of that load: during prefill it copies layer N+1's KV from host memory while the GPU computes layer N.

blocks.caption: Load time grows linearly with n; recompute grows faster, because of attention (L = 32 layers, d = 4096). With these numbers a host hit wins at every length, so there is no break-even prompt length, only a link speed below which recomputing wins (3.3 to 3.7 GB/s, see the optional offloading course).

blocks.prompt: Rerun scene 2 with `write_back` instead of `write_through`. When few-shot q1 needs room, what extra work appears, and what work disappears?
blocks.reveal: **A copy moves onto the critical path.** A1, A2 and B1 have no host copy yet, so their 430 tokens (about 56 MB, roughly 1.1 ms at 50 GB/s) must be copied down before their GPU slots can be reused. Under write_through that copy was made earlier, when each node was first cached. **What disappears** is copying nodes that are never evicted. In this trace that is only A turn 3's 130-token node: every other node is still copied, just later, when it is demoted (the few-shot nodes at B turn 2, for example), 1,475 tokens in all instead of 1,605. Write-back trades less copy bandwidth for copies at eviction time.

blocks.md:
The flags, at the pinned commit:

- `--enable-hierarchical-cache` (alias `--enable-hicache`) turns it on.
- `--hicache-ratio` sizes the host pool as a multiple of the GPU pool (default 2.0, lowered automatically if host memory is short); the docs say it must be above 1, because the host pool should be larger than the GPU pool (the code at the pinned commit only warns that L2 is less effective otherwise). `--hicache-size` gives gigabytes per rank instead.
- `--hicache-storage-backend` attaches L3: `file`, `mooncake` (Mooncake Store, the distributed KV store of Moonshot AI's Kimi serving platform), `hf3fs` (DeepSeek's 3FS distributed file system), `nixl` (NVIDIA's data-transfer library), `aibrix` (ByteDance's open-source serving control plane) and others.
- `--hicache-storage-prefetch-policy` decides how long a request waits for L3 (`best_effort`, `wait_complete`, or the default `timeout`); the optional *KV cache offloading* course walks through these.
- `--page-size` sets the transfer unit: bigger pages mean fewer, larger L3 objects but coarser matches.

blocks.md:
Which tier can another server see? L1 and L2 belong to one instance's process: two instances never read each other's host memory, not even on the same node. Only L3 can be shared, and only if the backend spans the instances: `file` writes to /tmp/hicache by default, which is node-local unless it is a shared mount, while Mooncake, 3FS, NIXL and AIBrix reach across a cluster when every instance uses the same namespace and configuration.

Under tensor parallelism the ranks agree on how many L3 tokens hit with an all-reduce that takes the minimum. For MLA models, whose KV is identical on every rank, only one rank writes it back. The LMSYS HiCache post reports up to 6x throughput and up to 80% lower TTFT in its own benchmarks (not run here).

Misconception: "a large `--hicache-ratio` pools the host memory of all my servers." It only makes each instance's own L2 bigger. Cross-instance reuse needs a shared L3 backend, and the router must still send related requests where the KV is cheapest to reach.

HiCache turns GPU eviction into demotion. The radix tree, match rules and leaves-first eviction stay the same; each node simply remembers which tiers hold its KV, and a hit in host memory costs a copy instead of a prefill.

blocks.question: Two SGLang instances run on different nodes, each with `--enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-ratio 4` and no storage backend. A chat's next turn is routed to the other instance than before. Why does it miss the cache?
options: The router hashes prompts, so the two instances never see the same prefix
Host memory (L2) is private to each instance; only an L3 backend that both instances share could carry the history across
A ratio of 4 is too small to hold a chat history
HiCache only keeps KV in host memory under the write_back policy
blocks.explain: L1 and L2 belong to one instance's process. The first instance may still hold the history in host memory, but the second cannot read it. Attaching a shared backend such as Mooncake or 3FS (with the same namespace on both) makes L3 hits possible; routing the turn back to the first instance also works.

blocks.question: Your host link is busy with L3 prefetch traffic, and most cached prefixes in your workload are used exactly once. Which write policy fits best?
options: write_through, so that every node already has a host copy when it is evicted
No HiCache at all: one-off prefixes can never benefit
write_back with a larger --hicache-ratio
write_through_selective, which copies a node only after it is hit again
blocks.explain: Selective write-through spends host bandwidth only on prefixes that proved reusable, so one-off prompts never cost a copy. Plain write_through copies everything, which wastes the busy link. write_back also skips copies until eviction, but then copies whatever is evicted, including one-off prefixes, on the eviction path.

lessons.title: Cache-aware scheduling: queue order sets the hit rate

blocks.md: A busy server has a **waiting queue**. Which requests it admits next decides what stays cached. If the scheduler alternates between unrelated prefixes, each one evicts the other before it can be reused: **cache thrashing**. The paper's fix is to sort the waiting queue by **matched prefix length**, longest first, instead of first come, first served (FCFS).

Algorithm 1 in the paper runs every scheduling step:

1. Match every waiting request against the radix tree and record its prefix length.
2. Sort by that length, longest first.
3. Admit requests while their uncached tokens fit in the space that is free or evictable, locking each admitted request's prefix so it cannot be evicted.
4. Allocate memory for the batch, evicting LRU leaves if needed, and run it.
5. For finished requests, unlock their nodes and insert their prompt and output.

A toy queue: three prefix groups A, B and C, each with a 240-token shared prefix, and three requests per group with 60 unique tokens each (300 per request). They arrive interleaved: A1, B1, C1, A2 and so on. The cache holds 400 tokens, enough for one group's prefix plus a request. A script ran each order one request at a time through the radix tree with LRU eviction.

blocks.title: Same nine requests, two orders

scenes.caption: Nine requests in three prefix groups, arriving interleaved. FCFS runs them as they came; longest prefix match (LPM) re-sorts the queue every step.
FCFS with a 400-token cache: each request evicts the previous group's prefix, so every request misses. 0 of 2700 prompt tokens hit.
LPM: A1 runs first (all tied at 0). Then A2 and A3 match 240 tokens, so they jump ahead of B1 and C1. Each group pays its prefix once: 1440 of 2700 tokens hit, 53.3%.
Grow the cache to 900 tokens, room for all three prefixes, and FCFS also reaches 53.3%. Order matters when the cache cannot hold every active prefix group at once.

blocks.md: Is 53.3% the best possible? Build the radix tree of the whole batch. Every edge's KV must be computed at least once, so the computed tokens are at least the sum of edge lengths. The paper proves that visiting the tree in **depth-first order** (the order a depth-first search, or DFS, takes: finish everything under one child before moving to the next) reaches this bound whenever the cache holds at least the longest request, and that longest-shared-prefix-first produces such an order (the reason is below). Here the edges are 3 prefixes of 240 plus 9 suffixes of 60: 1260 tokens out of 2700. Call this floor the **DFS bound**: at least 1260 tokens must be computed, so the best possible hit rate is 1 minus 1260 over 2700, which is 1440 over 2700, about 53.3%.

blocks.caption: The DFS bound in words: one minus the sum of the tree's edge lengths over the sum of all request lengths, here 1 minus 1260 over 2700. The cache (400) is larger than the longest request (300), so the theorem applies and LPM attains it.

blocks.md: Why is longest-prefix-first depth first? Say the scheduler just ran a request whose path ends at node v, so v and all its ancestors are cached. Every waiting request branches off that path somewhere, and the one sharing the longest cached prefix branches off deepest, nearest to v. So the next pick lies in the subtree of v, or of the nearest ancestor that still has waiting requests below it: a subtree is finished before the scheduler climbs out of it, which is exactly DFS order. Because the cache holds at least the longest request, the current path stays cached the whole time, so every edge is computed once and the bound above is met. In the toy, after A1 the A requests match 240 tokens and B1 and C1 match 0, so A2 and A3 go next.

blocks.title: Hit rate by scheduling order (toy queue)

scenes.caption: 400-token cache. Random orders (expected over all orders) get 17.8%; LPM matches the DFS optimum of 53.3%.
900-token cache. With room for every prefix, FCFS also reaches the optimum and random orders average 43.8% (expected over all orders).

blocks.md: A gap remains when nothing is cached yet. If four requests share a 240-token prefix and arrive together, every match is 0, and admitting all four in one batch prefills the prefix four times. Under the cache-aware policies the current scheduler adds **in-batch prefix caching**: it inserts waiting requests into a small simulated tree, and a request whose cache match is short (32 tokens or fewer by default) but which shares 32 or more tokens with an earlier waiting request is temporarily pushed back. One request runs first; the others hit its cached prefix on the next step.

blocks.prompt: Four requests with a shared 240-token prefix and 60 unique tokens each arrive at an empty cache. How many prompt tokens are computed if all four are admitted together, versus with in-batch deprioritization?
blocks.reveal: **1200 versus 480.** Together: 4 x 300 = 1200, since none can reuse a prefix that is still being computed. Deprioritized: the first request computes 300, then the other three compute only their 60 unique tokens each, 300 + 180 = 480. The cost is one extra scheduling step of latency for three of the requests.

blocks.md:
In the current runtime this lives behind `--schedule-policy`. The documented default is `fcfs`; the tuning guide suggests `lpm` (longest prefix match) when a workload has many shared prefixes, noting it adds scheduling overhead. Other options include `dfs-weight`, `lof` (longest output first), `random`, `priority` and `routing-key`, plus newer experimental ones.

Matching every waiting request costs CPU time, so under `lpm` with more than 128 waiting requests the scheduler stops sorting the whole queue and falls back to FCFS order. At the pinned commit it adds a bounded mode: every 32 scheduling passes it checks whether the first 64 waiting requests share long prefixes that would thrash the cache, and if so it sorts just that 64-request window by prefix length.

Greedy longest-prefix-first can **starve** a request whose prefix is never cached: requests that hit keep jumping ahead of it. The paper says so directly and leaves fair cache-aware scheduling as future work. Watch tail latency (the latency of the slowest requests, such as the 99th percentile) if you enable `lpm`.
Scheduling cannot create reuse; it can only avoid destroying it. The DFS bound (sum of tree edges) is the floor on prefill work, and ordering decides whether a tight cache reaches it.

blocks.question: You set `--schedule-policy lpm`, but under heavy load with about 500 waiting requests the hit rate looks the same as FCFS. What is the most likely reason?
options: LPM only works with a page size of 1
The radix tree is disabled whenever the queue is non-empty
LPM sorts by output length when the queue is long
With more than 128 waiting requests the scheduler stops matching the whole queue and falls back to FCFS (sorting at most a 64-request window) to bound its own overhead
blocks.explain: Matching every waiting request against the tree on every step costs CPU time that grows with the queue, so above 128 waiting requests the source uses FCFS order, at most sorting a 64-request window at the head when it detects thrashing risk. Keeping the queue shorter (or routing by prefix upstream) restores the effect.

blocks.question: In which situation does cache-aware ordering help least?
options: The cache comfortably holds every active prefix group at once
Many interleaved prefix groups compete for a small cache
A batch job of few-shot prompts that share examples in several groups
Multi-turn chats from many users on a memory-constrained GPU
blocks.explain: When everything fits, nothing useful is evicted, so any order reaches the optimum (FCFS reached 53.3% at 900 tokens in the toy). Ordering pays when the cache is too small for all groups and thrashing would otherwise occur.

lessons.title: Compressed FSMs: decoding several tokens in one step

blocks.md: **Constrained decoding** forces the output to match a format, such as a JSON schema written as a regular expression. The standard method (used by Outlines, an open-source Python library for structured generation) compiles the regex into a **finite state machine** (FSM): states plus transitions labeled with characters. At each decoding step the engine looks at the current state, sets the probability of every token that would break the pattern to zero (a logit mask), samples, and advances the state. A logit is the raw score the model gives each vocabulary token before softmax turns the scores into probabilities; the mask sets a banned token's logit to minus infinity, so its probability becomes exactly zero.

That method decodes one token per forward pass, even through text the format fixes completely. In a schema like `{"name": "...", "house": "...", "age": ...}`, the keys, quotes and punctuation are not choices at all, yet each of their tokens costs a full forward pass of the model.

SGLang's fix starts from a character-level FSM and compresses it. A **singular transition edge** is one whose source state has exactly one successor and which accepts exactly one character or string. Runs of consecutive singular edges are merged into one **compressed edge** labeled with their concatenated text. During decoding, whenever the current state begins a compressed edge, the runtime appends the whole string at once. The blog of LMSYS Org (the Large Model Systems Organization, where SGLang was announced) calls this **jump-forward decoding**.

Appending text is a prefill (extend) of the new tokens, not a decode. The implementation is short because of RadixAttention: the runtime ends the current request and enqueues a new one whose prompt is the old text plus the jumped string; the radix tree reuses all the earlier KV, so only the new tokens are computed, in the same pass that produces the next token's logits. The example below counts tokens with GPT-2's tokenizer, which uses byte-pair encoding (BPE): starting from single bytes, tokenizer training repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token, so common words and word pieces become single tokens.

blocks.title: Normal vs jump-forward decoding of one JSON object

scenes.caption: Output {"name": "Harry", "house": "Gryffindor", "age": 11} in GPT-2's BPE tokens (computed with tiktoken, OpenAI's tokenizer library; an underscore marks a space). Normal FSM decoding samples every token: 21 forward passes.
Tokens in gray contain only text the regex fixes; tokens in color contain a real choice. Only 5 of 21 do: the name, the closing quote, the first letter of the house, the age, and the closing brace.
Jump-forward: forced runs are appended without sampling. Pass 1 is the prompt prefill plus the first jump; passes 3 and 4 are extends that also carry a jump. 5 sampling passes instead of 21.

A boundary artifact: the jumped text ends with a space, which tokenizes as a lone space token. The model then emits 11 without a space, while normal decoding would have produced one token, space plus 11. Token boundaries change what the model sees.

blocks.prompt: The house field is `(Gryffindor|Hufflepuff|Ravenclaw|Slytherin)`. The model has just emitted the token `G`. What can the runtime do next?
blocks.reveal: Jump. Only one alternative starts with G, so the rest of the word, the closing quote, the comma and the next key are all fixed: `ryffindor", "age": ` is one compressed edge, 9 tokens appended in a single extend pass. The same works for any enum whose options diverge early.

blocks.caption: Counted for the example above (a simplified model: it assumes the model emits these exact tokens). Extend passes that carry jumped tokens do more work than a decode step, so time saved is smaller than 21/5.

blocks.md: Measured gains are smaller than the pass count suggests, because real outputs contain free text and extends are heavier than decodes. The LMSYS blog reports up to 2x lower latency and up to 2.5x higher throughput than guidance (Microsoft's constrained-generation library) running on llama.cpp (a C and C++ inference engine) and Outlines running on vLLM on JSON tasks; the paper's ablation measures 1.6x throughput from the compressed FSM on its JSON benchmark, and notes the FSM must be preprocessed once and reused across a batch.

Token boundaries are the hard part. A model may prefer to merge the closing quote with a comma into the single token `",`; if the regex ended right after the quote, that token would be masked and the model could keep generating instead of stopping. And tokenizing a jumped string on its own can split it in ways the model never saw in training (the paper's example: `summa` plus `ry`). So SGLang appends the jumped *string* and **retokenizes** the text, which the blog measured at about 4% overhead.

Jumping can distort choices. The paper's example: if the grade regex were `Excellent|Above Average|Fair|Below Average` and the model, intending a letter grade, emits `A`, the FSM jumps to `Above Average` even though the model never weighed that phrase. Listing the options in the prompt helps; the paper leaves exact probabilities as future work.

The ecosystem has moved since the paper. Current docs list three grammar backends (XGrammar, the default; Outlines; llguidance) covering JSON schema, regex and EBNF, chosen with `--grammar-backend`. XGrammar is a grammar engine from the MLC (Machine Learning Compilation) team behind the MLC LLM engine, llguidance is the Rust engine behind guidance, and EBNF (Extended Backus-Naur Form) is a standard notation that writes a grammar as named rewrite rules. The v0.4 release notes report up to 10x faster JSON decoding with XGrammar. Note that jump-forward itself is not active in current releases: at the pinned commit the general grammar backends no longer contain jump-forward code, so each output token is decoded with a grammar mask; the next lesson shows how that mask is built. The idea of this lesson still holds: the less the grammar leaves open, the fewer real sampling decisions a structured output needs.

blocks.question: Which constraint gives jump-forward decoding the largest saving?
options: A free-text field `[\w\s]{1,500}` with no other structure
A schema with long constant key names and enums whose options differ in their first character
A regex that accepts any digit sequence
Plain decoding with no constraint at all
blocks.explain: Savings come from compressed edges: text the grammar fully determines. Long keys and early-diverging enums create long forced runs. Free text and open digit runs leave a real choice at every token, so nothing can be skipped.

blocks.question: Why does SGLang retokenize after a jump instead of appending the jumped string's own tokens?
options: Retokenizing is the only way to compute logits
The jumped string has no tokens until the detokenizer runs
Tokenizing the jumped piece alone can give splits the model rarely saw (summa plus ry), shifting its next-token distribution; retokenizing keeps the context close to normal
To make the KV cache smaller
blocks.explain: Models are trained on canonical BPE tokenizations. A non-canonical boundary changes the input the model conditions on. The paper and blog retokenize the text to keep it aligned, at a small cost.

lessons.title: Structured output today: grammar masks inside the SGLang scheduler

blocks.md:
Ask a model for `{"name": string, "age": integer}`. At the first step only 2 of GPT-2's 50,257 vocabulary tokens are legal, `{` and `{"`; inside the name string almost all of them are; after `"age":` only tokens that start a number. Every step therefore needs a fresh **token mask**: one bit per vocabulary token, 1 if the grammar allows it. The sampler sets the logits of masked tokens to minus infinity, as lesson 5 described.

With jump-forward off, this mask is the whole mechanism of structured output in SGLang. XGrammar, the default backend, builds it.

How XGrammar builds masks fast is taught in the *LLM prompting and structured output* course (lesson 5, optional reading outside this course's prerequisites): the schema becomes a grammar run by a **pushdown automaton**, an FSM plus a stack (nested JSON needs memory that grows with depth, which no FSM has); masks for tokens whose validity depends only on the current position are precomputed, and only the few tokens that close a rule are checked against the stack at run time.

This lesson covers what SGLang does around that engine: when grammars are compiled, where in the loop the mask is computed, and what that costs. First, real masks.

blocks.code:
import json, time
import xgrammar as xgr
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2")            # 50,257-token vocabulary
info = xgr.TokenizerInfo.from_huggingface(tok)
compiler = xgr.GrammarCompiler(info, max_threads=2)
schema = json.dumps({"type": "object", "additionalProperties": False,
    "properties": {"name": {"type": "string"}, "age": {"type": "integer"}},
    "required": ["name", "age"]})

t0 = time.perf_counter(); grammar = compiler.compile_json_schema(schema)
t1 = time.perf_counter(); compiler.compile_json_schema(schema)  # cached
t2 = time.perf_counter()
print(f"compile {1e3*(t1-t0):.1f} ms, again {1e3*(t2-t1):.3f} ms")

matcher = xgr.GrammarMatcher(grammar)
mask = xgr.allocate_token_bitmask(1, info.vocab_size)    # 1 bit per token
times = []
for i, t in enumerate(tok.encode('{"name": "Ada", "age": 36}')):
    s = time.perf_counter()
    matcher.fill_next_token_bitmask(mask)                # CPU work per step
    times.append(time.perf_counter() - s)
    banned = len(xgr.testing._get_masked_tokens_from_bitmask(mask, info.vocab_size))
    print(f"step {i:2d} allowed {info.vocab_size - banned:6d} then emit {tok.decode([t])!r}")
    assert matcher.accept_token(t)                       # advance the automaton
print(f"mask per step: median {1e6*sorted(times)[len(times)//2]:.0f} us, max {1e6*max(times):.0f} us")
blocks.caption: Run here on CPU (xgrammar 0.2.9, GPT-2's tokenizer from Hugging Face, OMP_NUM_THREADS=2). Allowed per step, the same every run: 2, 4, 5, 67, 50032, 50032, 50032, 7, 3, 3, 1602, 1001. Timings from one run (they vary): compile 1.5 ms, again 0.008 ms; mask median 5 us, max 21 us.

blocks.title: Legal tokens per step for {"name": string, "age": integer}

scenes.caption: XGrammar's mask for each step of the output {"name": "Ada", "age": 36}, counted with GPT-2's tokenizer (an underscore marks a space). The mask is rebuilt before every token.
Keys and punctuation: 2 to 67 legal tokens. The grammar nearly fixes the text, yet with jump-forward off each of these tokens still costs a full decode step.
Inside the name string almost everything is legal (50,032 tokens): only tokens that would break the string, such as raw control characters, are masked.

The integer: 1,602 tokens are legal here, almost all digit runs with or without a leading space, plus whitespace and a minus sign. After 36, the 1,001 legal tokens are more digits, whitespace or the closing brace.

blocks.md: **Compile once, then cache.** A request that carries `json_schema`, `regex` or `ebnf` first enters the scheduler's **grammar queue**. Compilation runs in a background thread pool, and the result is cached under the constraint's text, so the next request with the same schema skips it (in the run above: 1.5 ms the first time, under 0.01 ms from the cache; large schemas take much longer). A request moves on to the waiting queue once its grammar is ready. Invalid grammars are cached too, so repeats fail fast.

**Mask inside the overlapped loop.** Lesson 7's overlap scheduler launches step k+1 before the CPU has looked at step k's tokens. A grammar request cannot be sampled that blindly: the mask for k+1 depends on the token sampled at k, which must first be fed into the automaton (`accept_token`).

So SGLang splits the step for grammar requests. It launches the forward pass of k+1 at once, because the forward pass does not need the mask. Then the CPU processes step k's results, advancing every grammar. Only then does it launch the sampling of k+1, with a mask built from the advanced grammars. The long forward pass still overlaps the CPU work; only sampling waits.

blocks.title: Two grammar-constrained steps, without and with overlap (toy numbers)

scenes.caption: Toy costs: 1.5 ms of CPU work per step (process results, advance grammars, plan), 0.5 ms to fill the masks, 10 ms forward pass, 0.5 ms sampling. In series: 12.5 ms per step, 25 ms for two.

Overlapped: forward 1 launches at once. During it the CPU processes step 0 (0.5 ms), fills mask 1 (0.5 ms) and plans step 2 (1 ms): the same 2 ms of CPU work per step as above, now hidden. Only sampling waits: two steps end at 22.5 ms.

blocks.md:
Two more details from the source. Under tensor parallelism every rank holds its own copy of each grammar, and when grammars are present the sampled tokens are synchronized across ranks so that all copies advance identically. Speculative decoding (lesson 9) builds its own mask over the whole draft tree during verification.

The mask cost in the run above, a median of about 5 and at most about 21 microseconds per request per step on a laptop CPU (a rerun gave medians of 4 to 10), is small next to a forward pass of several milliseconds, which is why hiding it behind the forward pass is enough. Compilation is the cost to watch: it runs once per distinct schema.

# Not run here: needs a running server (python -m sglang.launch_server ...)
import openai
client = openai.Client(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:30000/v1", api_key="None")
schema = {"type": "object",
          "properties": {"name": {"type": "string"},
                         "population": {"type": "integer"}},
          "required": ["name", "population"]}
resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content":
               "Give the capital of France as JSON with name and population."}],
    temperature=0, max_tokens=128,
    response_format={"type": "json_schema",

print(resp.choices[0].message.content)
blocks.caption: The OpenAI-compatible form, following SGLang's structured outputs docs. The native /generate API takes the same constraint as `json_schema`, `regex` or `ebnf` in `sampling_params`; only one per request.

blocks.md:
Choosing a backend with `--grammar-backend`:

- `xgrammar` (the default) supports JSON schema, regex and EBNF.
- `llguidance` supports JSON schema, regex and EBNF.
- `outlines` supports JSON schema and regex, but not EBNF.
- `none` disables constrained decoding.

The docs recommend XGrammar for performance, and advise describing the expected format in the prompt as well: the mask can forbid a token but cannot tell the model what a field means.

A mask makes output *legal*, not *fast*. Forced keys and punctuation still cost one decode step per token (7 of the 12 steps above had 67 or fewer legal tokens). Short key names and compact schemas save real time; long descriptive keys cost a forward pass per token.

In SGLang a grammar costs three things: a compile per distinct schema (hidden by the cache after the first request), a CPU mask per request per step (hidden behind the forward pass by delaying only the sampling), and one decode step per forced token.

blocks.question: With the overlap scheduler on, SGLang launches the forward pass of a grammar request's step k+1 before step k's token has been processed, but holds back its sampling. Why that split?
options: The forward pass does not depend on the grammar, but the mask for k+1 needs the automaton advanced by step k's token
Sampling is slower than the forward pass, so it must be delayed to balance the GPU
The grammar must be recompiled after every token
Tensor-parallel ranks cannot run sampling at the same time
blocks.explain: Logits for step k+1 only need the input token, which the GPU already has. The mask, though, is a function of the grammar state after accepting step k's token, which happens on the CPU while the forward pass runs. Delaying only the sampling keeps the overlap and keeps masks correct.

blocks.question: A service sends 10,000 requests, each with a different, freshly generated JSON schema, and sees much higher time to first token than with one fixed schema. What is the most likely cause?
options: The radix cache cannot store JSON outputs
Masks for unique schemas are computed on the GPU instead of the CPU
XGrammar falls back to jump-forward decoding for new schemas
Every request waits in the grammar queue for its own compilation, because the grammar cache only helps when a schema repeats
blocks.explain: Compilation is per distinct constraint and runs before the request can be scheduled. A fixed schema compiles once and then hits the cache. Reusing schemas (for example, generating them from a few templates) removes the cost.

blocks.question: Your application needs an EBNF grammar for a small domain-specific language. Which `--grammar-backend` cannot serve it?
options: xgrammar
outlines
llguidance
None of them: SGLang supports only JSON schema
blocks.explain: The docs list EBNF support for XGrammar and llguidance; Outlines in SGLang supports JSON schema and regex only.

lessons.title: Inside the server: three processes and an overlapped loop

blocks.md:
The SGLang Runtime splits serving into processes that talk through sockets of ZeroMQ (ZMQ), a lightweight message-passing library, according to the docstring of its `Engine` class:

- **TokenizerManager**, in the main process with the HTTP server: tokenizes requests, sends them on, and returns results to clients.
- **Scheduler**, a subprocess (one per tensor-parallel rank: with tensor parallelism, covered in lesson 8, each layer's weights are split across GPUs and each GPU's share is driven by its own process, called a rank): owns the radix cache and KV pool, forms batches, runs the model, and sends output token ids onward.
- **DetokenizerManager**, a subprocess: turns token ids back into text increments and returns them to the TokenizerManager.

Keeping tokenization and detokenization out of the scheduler's process keeps that CPU work off the loop that feeds the GPU.

blocks.title: One streaming request through the runtime

scenes.caption: The client posts a prompt over HTTP. The TokenizerManager turns it into token ids and sends it to the scheduler over ZMQ.
The scheduler matches the prompt against the radix tree, admits it into a prefill batch, and runs the forward pass.
Sampled token ids for the whole batch go to the DetokenizerManager, which decodes text incrementally and sends it back.
Every decode step repeats the scheduler to detokenizer to tokenizer hop. When the request finishes, its prompt and output are inserted into the radix tree for later reuse.

blocks.md: The scheduler's loop is simple in outline: take in new requests, choose a batch, run it, process the results. Choosing the batch is where the policy lives. Requests that finished prefill join the running batch; then the scheduler tries to build a **new prefill batch**, and only if there is none does it run a **decode step** for every running request. If the KV pool fills during decoding, it **retracts** some requests back to the queue; the tuning guide treats occasional retraction as normal and suggests raising `--schedule-conservativeness` if it is frequent.

blocks.title: The scheduler loop (simplified from scheduler.py)

scenes.caption: Each iteration first pulls new requests that the TokenizerManager sent.
Requests whose prefill just finished move into the running batch, where they will decode.
The policy orders the queue and admits what fits in free plus evictable KV memory. A prefill batch takes priority over decoding.
Run it on the GPU, then hand the sampled tokens to the detokenizer.
Next iteration, with nothing new to prefill, all running requests decode one token. If memory runs out, some are retracted to the queue.

blocks.md: Every step of that loop has CPU work: scheduling, memory allocation, prefix matching. The v0.4 release notes say an unoptimized engine can spend as much as half its time on CPU overhead. The **overlap scheduler** ("zero-overhead batch scheduler") runs the CPU one batch ahead: while the GPU executes batch k, the CPU prepares batch k+1. The catch is that batch k+1's input tokens are batch k's outputs, which do not exist yet; SGLang uses placeholder **future tokens** that the GPU resolves when the previous step finishes. It is on by default (`--disable-overlap-schedule` turns it off).

blocks.title: Four decode steps, without and with overlap (toy numbers)

scenes.caption: Toy model: 3 ms of CPU scheduling and 10 ms of GPU work per step. Run in series, the GPU idles 3 of every 13 ms (23%) and four steps take 52 ms.
Overlapped: planning for step k+1 runs while the GPU executes step k, with future tokens standing in for unsampled outputs. Only the first plan is exposed: 43 ms, about 1.2x faster in this toy.

blocks.md: How can the CPU build a batch whose inputs do not exist yet? In the current source (class `FutureMap` in `overlap_utils.py`) the answer is an index. Every running request owns a slot in the request pool, and the GPU keeps a buffer with one entry per slot. After sampling step k, the GPU writes each request's token into its slot's entry. Step k+1 is built on the CPU with no token ids at all, only slot numbers, and its first GPU operation reads its inputs from the buffer at those slots. Both run on the same GPU stream, in order, so the read always sees the write and the CPU never waits for the token.

blocks.title: Two overlapped decode steps with future tokens (simplified)
blocks.code:
# Simplified from scheduler.py (event_loop_overlap)
# and overlap_utils.py (FutureMap)
buf = gpu_empty(pool_size)     # one entry per request slot

def launch(batch):             # queues GPU work, returns at once
    if batch.input_ids is None:          # a decode batch
        batch.input_ids = buf[batch.slots]   # gather on GPU
    tokens = sample(forward(batch))
    buf[batch.slots] = tokens            # scatter on GPU
    return copy_to_cpu_async(tokens)

def process(batch, result):    # CPU, one step late
    tokens = result.wait()     # waits for that step only
    for req, tok in zip(batch.reqs, tokens):
        if req.left_batch:     # finished earlier: drop extra
            continue
        req.append(tok)        # stream text, advance grammar
        if tok == EOS or hits_stop(req):
            req.finish()       # but it is already in flight

last = None
while True:
    batch = build_next_batch()   # slots only, input_ids None
    result = launch(batch)       # GPU starts this step
    if last:
        process(*last)           # previous step's results
    last = (batch, result)

scenes.caption: Step k is already on the GPU for R1 (slot 3) and R2 (slot 5). The CPU builds step k+1 without knowing step k's tokens: the batch holds only slot numbers.
launch queues step k+1 behind step k on the same GPU stream. Its first operation gathers buf[3] and buf[5], which step k's scatter will have written by then.
Step k finishes on the GPU: it sampled cat for R1 and EOS for R2 and scattered them into the buffer. Step k+1 reads them without any CPU round trip.
Meanwhile the CPU processes step k, one step late: R1 appends cat; R2 hit EOS and finishes. But R2 is already inside step k+1, which is running.
Next iteration: step k+1's results are processed. R2 left the batch, so its extra token is dropped and its slot freed. Only R1 continues.

blocks.md: What still has to wait? Everything that needs the token on the CPU: stop checks (EOS, stop strings), streaming text to the client, advancing grammars, freeing finished requests' memory, and retraction decisions all run in `process` for step k while step k+1 is already on the GPU. A request that finishes at step k therefore rides along in step k+1 and its extra token is thrown away. Requests that will finish by length are known in advance, so the scheduler leaves them out of the next batch.

The measured gain was modest because SGLang's scheduler was already lean: v0.4 reported 1.1x throughput over v0.3, largest on small models and large tensor-parallel sizes, and a profile from Nsight, NVIDIA's GPU profiler, with no GPU idle time between five consecutive decode batches.

**Chunked prefill** splits a long prompt into pieces of at most `--chunked-prefill-size` tokens, processed over several loop iterations (the scheduler keeps one partially prefilled request). When unset, the current source picks the size from GPU memory, from 2048 tokens on GPUs under 20 GB up to 16384 on the largest; `-1` disables it. The docs' advice: if prefill of long prompts runs out of memory, lower it. With `--enable-mixed-chunk`, running decodes join each chunk's batch, the piggybacking idea from the Sarathi paper (Agrawal et al., 2023). Piggybacking means the decodes, one token each, ride in a forward pass that runs anyway for the chunk, instead of waiting for a pass of their own.

blocks.title: A 6000-token prompt arrives while 8 requests decode (toy model)

scenes.caption: Toy cost: 10 ms per step plus 0.01 ms per prefill token. Unchunked, the prompt is one 70 ms step, and the gap between the 8 requests' tokens grows from 10 ms to 80 ms.

Chunks of 2048: three steps of 30.48, 30.48 and 29.04 ms. Each forward pass is bounded, but in the prefill-first loop the decodes still wait: a 100 ms gap, and the prompt's first token comes 20 ms later.

Mixed chunks: the 8 decodes ride along in every chunk's batch (their few tokens add little compute here). Their token gap is about 30 ms instead of 80, at the cost of a later first token for the long prompt.

blocks.md: Chunked prefill trades the long prompt's time to first token for bounded step size: lower peak activation memory (activations are the intermediate tensors a forward pass keeps, and they grow with the number of tokens in the pass) and, when decodes are mixed in, steadier token gaps for everyone else. It does not reduce total prefill work.

To see these numbers on a real server, launch one with metrics on, send load with shared prefixes, and read the scheduler's log. Each prefill step logs a line such as `Prefill batch, #new-seq: 4, #new-token: 512, #cached-token: 8192, token usage: 0.41, #running-req: 60, #queue-req: 12`, where #new-token counts tokens actually prefilled and #cached-token tokens matched in the radix tree. Decode steps log `#running-req`, `token usage` (the fraction of the KV pool held by requests; evictable cached tokens count as free), `cuda graph`, generation throughput and `#queue-req`. Retraction shows up as the warning `KV cache pool is full. Retract requests.` The same values appear at `/metrics` as `sglang:cache_hit_rate`, `sglang:num_running_reqs`, `sglang:num_queue_reqs`, `sglang:token_usage` and `sglang:num_retracted_reqs`.
